extracted.intended_audience: experimental natural philosophers / members of learned societies (e.g., Royal Society), instrument makers, anatomists, experimentalists
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and conducting empirical experiments and instrument descriptions in natural philosophy (magnetism, respiration, anatomy, instrumentation, metallurgy), with procedural detail, measurements, and demonstrations for learned-society audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of magnetic specimens (homogeneity and balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare the magnet/stone spherical, compact and uniform so its three centres (magnitude, gravity, and magnetism) coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a spherical magnet with emery powder about 1-1/2 inch diameter; find poles exactly, make two small holes to support it on two needle points as pivots; place in a meridian of brass and suspend between pivots so it moves freely. Verify it has no preferential side due to gravity; if properly prepared a white mark on the stone remains fixed and it does not turn of itself. Anti-pattern: using a magnet with unequal centres so gravity biases its motion (which can falsify conclusions about motion/rotation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meridian tracing and azimuthal measurement for accurate declination
rubrics_metrics.description: Trace meridian lines by many azimuth observations, taken before and after noon, using suitably large and accurate instruments (e.g., a brass quadrant of six feet diameter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine true meridian by multiple azimuths rather than single measurements; use a large, well-divided quadrant for higher precision. The text emphasizes repeated azimuth measurements across times of day to reduce error from instrument or observation. Scoring note: accuracy improves with instrument size and repeated azimuth observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and specification of 'good' needles and instrument consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply good needles of known lengths (example: seven and ten inches) and, when possible, use the same needles across repeated measures to compare declinations reliably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare declination using well-made needles and, when testing secular or local variation, re-use the same needles to ensure comparability. Anti-pattern: relying on poorly constructed or differently sized needles which can produce spurious differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat observations across places and times to detect variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Make repeated observations in different places and over years to detect changes in magnetic declination and local differences (even miles apart).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare historical observations (e.g., Burrowes, Gunter, Gellibrand) and recent measures to reveal temporal trends; note that variation is continuous and differs by place—Whitehall and Limehouse differ despite close proximity. Recommendation: societies should observe and publish local magnetic direction at least annually to document changes over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument stability, rigidity, and anti-shake construction (micrometer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct measuring instruments (e.g., micrometer) to be steady and free from shake: rigid box, well-fitted screws and sockets, stiff indices and handles, and secure fastenings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design features include a small oblong brass box to contain screws and sockets, a springing plate to hold index without shake, stiff index fixed on a cylindrical part of the screw-head, and screws fixed so 'there appears not the least danger of shaking.' Alignment and minimization of play are essential. Anti-pattern: loose fittings or shaky screws reduce measurement reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of coarse and fine screw-threads and indexed divisions for high precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine a coarser screw for larger movements and a finer screw (and circular plate divided into 100 parts) to achieve fine measurement resolution; use indices to count coarse threads and the plate to read fine fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a screw with 60 threads for coarse movement, an outer circular plate divided into 100 parts for fractional revolutions, and an index to show how many threads separate sights. Ensure mid-point between sights remains on optical axis regardless of screw turns. Scoring note: correct reading requires counting revolutions (coarse) and reading plate divisions (fine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of sights with optical axis
rubrics_metrics.description: When attaching a micrometer or sighting device to a telescope, ensure the mid-point between sights lies in the axis of the glass so that sights open/close symmetrically about the optical axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach the plate to the telescope such that, however the screw is turned, the midst between the sights will always be in the axis. This preserves measurement geometry and avoids parallax errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document design, parts, and figures for complex instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide clear figures and step-by-step descriptions of instrument parts and their function when describing new instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The micrometer is described with numbered figures and each part (box, plate, screws, sights, indexes, tubes) is explained. Cross-reference previous descriptions (e.g., 'see No. 25, p. 161') for continued documentation. Inclusion of figures aids reproducibility and construction by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental demonstration, spectator verification, and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Show key physiological experiments publicly to judicious spectators, repeat trials, and demonstrate reproducibility when previous attempts by others have failed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Hooke repeated his dog respiration experiment before the learned society because others doubted earlier results; experiments were repeated many times with observers present. This strengthens credibility. Anti-pattern: claiming effects without public demonstration or independent repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control experiments to separate mechanical motion from exchange of fresh air
rubrics_metrics.description: Design controls that separate lung motion from supply of fresh air to determine which factor is essential for life (e.g., keep lungs constantly full but motionless vs allow motion without fresh air).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hooke used two bellows to keep lungs always full and motionless while observing heart and eyes; pricked the lung coat to let air escape and observed outcomes when blasts ceased. Lower's surgical nerve-cutting experiments further isolate diaphragm nerve function. Conclusion established: mechanical motion alone is insufficient; fresh air supply is necessary. Good control design demonstrates causality rather than correlation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological measurement and observation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor multiple physiological signs (heart beat, eye activity, convulsions, circulation through lungs) as outcome measures in respiration experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess life signs such as eye quickness, heart regularity, presence of convulsive fits when blasts cease, and blood circulation through lung tissue (e.g., after cutting a piece). Use such observations to support mechanistic claims about respiration and circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgical procedure and safety for nerve-isolation experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow precise surgical steps to isolate and cut nerves controlling the diaphragm while avoiding damage to lungs; practice on dead animals first to learn anatomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: pierce between 6th and 7th rib just into cavity, insert director/quill, cut intercostal muscles about an inch to avoid touching lungs, insert finger and separate nerve passing along the side of the pericardium toward the diaphragm, pull nerve to orifice, cut it off and sew the hole closely. Advice: first examine nerves in dead animals to be prepared. Emphasizes careful technique and anatomical familiarity to avoid confounding damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed anatomical description with measurements and microscopy
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting dissections, record detailed morphological features (counts of lobes, lengths, relative sizes), and use magnification where helpful (e.g., microscope to view tongue points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include reporting number of lung lobes, lengths of gut and tail, structure of teeth and tongue, microscopic observation of tongue points appearing transparent like crystal. Measurements and comparative notes (e.g., brain size vs other species) support anatomical conclusions and comparisons across taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stepwise, mechanistic description of production techniques (e.g., smelting lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe production processes in sequence with materials, apparatus, and operations: ore location, preparation, washing, sifting, hearth construction, fuel, bellows usage, melting and casting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example procedure: ore lies in veins as a wall; ore beaten small, washed in running stream, sifted in iron rudders; furnace made of clay or fire-stone set in ground; fire lit with charcoal and continued with young oaken branches, blown with bellows by men's treading; molten lead taken with iron ladle and cast upon sand. Also note occupational hazards (smoke causes disease). Such procedural descriptions enable replication and highlight health considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative evaluation of competing hypotheses by weighing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Review multiple existing opinions on a topic, examine each, and favour the hypothesis best supported by empirical, geographical, or natural-history evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the author lists 18 opinions on ambergris, examines them, and prefers the one matching known geographic occurrences (e.g., relation to sea mammals or birds in Madagascar). Emphasize examining distributional and natural-history facts before adopting a hypothesis; remain cautious when evidence is incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument modification for user convenience and improved measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggest and test practical modifications (e.g., substituting hairs/threads for solid sight edges, adjusting rests/screw orientations) when they improve convenience without sacrificing accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example recommendations: fit sights with hairs/threads instead of solid edges for convenience; alter the rest so the screw is parallel to the equinoctial for simpler operation. Balance convenience improvements against potential impacts on precision; test modifications empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation for routine publication of local observational data
rubrics_metrics.description: Learned societies should observe and publish the state of magnetic direction in their locations at least annually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular publication allows tracking secular and local variations in magnetic declination and facilitates comparison across places and years. This is a community-standard recommendation to improve the body of observational evidence.
